claims.text: Conventionally cast and annealed bulk MnNiSi-based magnetic refrigerants can have a single-phase structure and a large magnetocaloric effect but poor mechanical strength.
Controlled cold working followed by two-step annealing can nucleate nanoscale precipitates in the MnNiSi matrix.
The proposed thermomechanical treatment can produce a uniform precipitate distribution.
Annealing near but below the transformation temperature followed by rapid cooling will favor fine precipitates and prevent coarsening.
Precipitates smaller than approximately 50 nm and at moderate volume fraction can be introduced without shifting or broadening the magnetostructural transition.
Uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates act as dislocation-pinning centers.
Uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates reinforce grain boundaries and produce a refined microstructure.
Nanoscale precipitates obstruct dislocation motion and thereby increase yield strength.
Nanoscale precipitates inhibit grain growth and thereby increase toughness.
The proposed precipitates are magnetically inactive.
A moderate volume fraction of magnetically inactive precipitates will not disrupt the magnetostructural transition responsible for the magnetocaloric effect.
Thermomechanical treatment will increase the yield strength of the MnNiSi-based alloy relative to conventional casting and annealing.
Thermomechanical treatment will improve fracture toughness relative to conventional casting and annealing.
The treated alloy will retain nearly the same peak magnetic entropy change and transition sharpness as the conventionally processed baseline.
Keeping precipitates below approximately 50 nm and below 10% total volume is an effective operating boundary for preserving the magnetocaloric transition.
Over-precipitation or precipitate coarsening can compromise the magnetocaloric transition or alter the transformation temperature.
